review.notes: Built on the course: complex sale, MEDDIC/MEDDPICC elements and 0-2 scoring, pursue/reset/walk, pain vs nice-to-have, pain chain, SPIN, value drivers, baseline/target/gap, ROI, payback, cost of inaction. Calculations checked. Fictional companies.

content.company: TrackWise Systems (fictional), selling fleet-tracking software; the prospect is Summit Brewing (fictional), with 180 delivery trucks
content.briefing: Summit Brewing could be your biggest deal this year: Kz 120 m. The sales cycle may take 6 months and involve many people. Your manager reviews the deal weekly using MEDDIC.

variants.text: Your contact is the fleet supervisor. He loves the demo. Who is the economic buyer?

choices.t: The person who can approve the money
choices.f: Likely the CFO or COO. You ask the supervisor who signs off spend this size.

choices.t: The fleet supervisor, who loves it
choices.f: Enthusiasm is not budget authority.

choices.t: The IT team, who will install it
choices.f: IT may influence; it rarely owns the budget.

variants.text: MEDDIC score for the deal (0 unknown, 1 assumed, 2 confirmed): Metrics 1, Economic buyer 0, Decision criteria 2, Decision process 0, Pain 2, Champion 1. Total and verdict?

choices.t: 6 of 12: reset before investing more
choices.f: Real pain, but no access to the economic buyer and unknown process.

choices.t: 6 of 12: commit it in the forecast
choices.f: Half unknown is not commit-ready.

choices.t: 8 of 12: pursue at full speed

variants.text: Who is a real champion?

choices.t: Someone with influence who sells for you inside
choices.f: A champion has power, gains from your success, and acts when you are not there.

choices.t: Anyone who is friendly and replies fast
choices.f: A friendly coach is not a champion without influence.

choices.t: The most senior person you have met
choices.f: Seniority without commitment is not championship.

variants.text: The deal has no clear pain and no path to the budget owner after 3 months.

choices.t: Walk away or park it, and free your time
choices.f: No pain and no buyer means low odds. Focus elsewhere.

choices.t: Keep pushing; persistence wins
choices.f: Time spent here is taken from winnable deals.

choices.t: Offer a 30% discount to create pain
choices.f: Discounts do not create a business problem.

variants.text: The customer says: 'It would be nice to see trucks on a map.' Is this pain?

choices.t: Not yet: pain needs a cost and an owner
choices.f: Dig into why it matters before treating it as pain.

choices.t: Yes: they clearly asked for the feature
choices.f: A wish is a nice-to-have.

choices.t: Yes, as long as they have a budget
choices.f: Budget helps, but without cost and owner it is still not pain.

variants.text: They mention late deliveries. Using the pain chain, what do you find next?

choices.t: Find cause, impact, owner and yearly cost
choices.f: Late deliveries come from poor routing; they cost Kz 4 m a month in fines.

choices.t: Present your routing module straight away
choices.f: Too early; the pain is not quantified.

choices.t: Ask how many trucks they run each day
choices.f: A situation question you could research.

variants.text: Which is an implication question?

choices.t: 'What do late deliveries cost you each month?'
choices.f: It links the problem to business impact.

choices.t: 'How many trucks do you run?'
choices.f: A situation question.

choices.t: 'Do you have problems with routing?'
choices.f: A problem question.

variants.text: How do you quantify the pain in discovery?

choices.t: Use the customer's own numbers
choices.f: Their numbers make the case credible to their CFO.

choices.t: Use industry averages from your slides
choices.f: Useful as a check, but less convincing than their data.

choices.t: Estimate high to make the case stronger
choices.f: Inflated numbers collapse under CFO review.

variants.text: Total benefit over 3 years: Kz 360 m. Total cost: Kz 120 m. What is the ROI?

choices.f: That is benefit / cost, not the return.
That divides by benefit instead of cost.

variants.text: Investment Kz 120 m. Monthly benefit Kz 10 m. What is the payback period?

choices.t: 12 months
10 months
choices.f: Recheck: 120 divided by 10 is 12.

choices.t: 36 months
choices.f: That is the contract length, not payback.

variants.text: Fines for late delivery cost Summit Kz 4 m a month. They want to delay the decision by 6 months.

choices.t: Show the cost of inaction: about Kz 24 m
choices.f: Every month of delay costs the buyer. Urgency becomes concrete.

choices.t: Offer a discount if they sign now
choices.f: Discounts create urgency at your cost; their own loss is stronger.

choices.t: Accept the delay politely
choices.f: Without urgency, deals stall.

variants.text: On-time delivery today is 78%; the target is 95%. How do you present the case?

choices.t: Baseline, target, gap and its value
choices.f: 17 points of gap, worth Kz 48 m a year in avoided fines.

choices.t: List all software features
choices.f: Features do not show value.

choices.t: Promise 100% on-time delivery
choices.f: Overpromising destroys credibility.

variants.text: Into which value driver does 'fewer accidents and insurance claims' fit?

choices.t: Reduce risk
choices.f: Revenue, cost or risk: every benefit fits one.

choices.t: Increase revenue
choices.f: Accidents are about risk and cost, not sales.

choices.t: None of the drivers
choices.f: Every benefit should fit one driver.

variants.text: Who should own the numbers in the business case?

choices.t: The customer, agreed with your champion
choices.f: Customer-owned numbers survive internal review.

choices.t: Your own marketing team, for speed
choices.f: Vendor numbers are discounted by buyers.

choices.t: Nobody; keeping them vague is safer
choices.f: Vague cases do not get approved.

variants.text: You don't know how Summit approves purchases this size. What do you ask your champion?

choices.t: The steps, people and dates to signature
choices.f: Decision process: technical review, CFO, board, legal.

choices.t: Whether they are happy with our price
choices.f: Price is not the process.

choices.t: Nothing; it will become clear later
choices.f: Unknown processes kill forecasts.

variants.text: Legal and procurement review will take 6 weeks after the business approves. Which MEDDPICC letter is this?

choices.t: P: paper process
choices.f: Plan it early so the deal does not slip at the end.

choices.t: C: competition
choices.f: Competition is about rival vendors.

choices.t: M: metrics
choices.f: Metrics are the measurable benefits.

variants.text: A rival vendor is also bidding. What do you do?

choices.t: Learn their position and shape decision criteria
choices.f: Competition is part of MEDDICC; criteria favour your strengths.

choices.t: Criticise the rival to the customer
choices.f: Attacking competitors hurts your credibility.

choices.t: Ignore them; focus on your demo
choices.f: Unknown competition is a blind spot.

variants.text: Your manager asks if the deal is 'commit' for this quarter. Economic buyer not met, paper process unknown.

choices.t: No: keep it as best case for now
choices.f: Commit needs evidence: buyer access and a known process.

choices.t: Yes: the champion is confident
choices.f: Confidence is not evidence.

choices.t: Yes, to meet the quarter target
choices.f: Forecasting to target, not evidence, damages trust.

variants.text: How do you prepare for the first discovery meeting?

choices.t: Research, agree agenda and time, plan questions
choices.f: You avoid asking facts you could have found yourself.

choices.t: Prepare a 40-slide product pitch
choices.f: Discovery is about listening, not pitching.

choices.t: Just turn up and chat
choices.f: Unprepared meetings waste the buyer's time.

variants.text: A need-payoff question sounds like:

choices.t: 'If this were fixed, what would it be worth?'
choices.f: The buyer states the value in their own words.

choices.t: 'Our tool fixes this, doesn't it?'
choices.f: A leading pitch, not a question.

choices.t: 'How long have you had trucks?'
choices.f: A situation question.
